newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine 3-yr bonds good idea, but not yet-dealers.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine 3-yr bonds good idea, but not yet-dealers.

text.p: The success of Ukraine's plans to sell one billion hryvnias ($539.4 million) of three-year bonds will depend on whether Ukraine passes the 1997 budget and gets a multi-billion International Monetary Fund credit, analysts said on Tuesday.
"Until Ukraine has a budget and IMF credit, they won't get any interest" in the bonds, said Jurgen Conrad, an economist with Deutsche Bank Research.

The government has not said when sales would start of the fixed-rate interest-bearing OVDZ government bonds, which will pay 15-percent interest in the first year and nine percent in years two and three.
Ukraine is due to pass the 1997 budget this month, fulfilling one of 41 conditions the IMF has set before releasing a $2.5 to $3 billion Extended Fund Facility loan.
Conrad said it was natural that Ukraine, planning to launch its first foreign bonds on the Japanese market in September, would also want to introduce domestic instruments.

"With a three-year IMF programme credit and the foreign bond, the picture will be totally different," he said, adding investors would be afraid to bet beyond the unofficial currency corridor, or trading band, of 1.70-90 hryvnias to the dollar.

"The unofficial corridor is given to the end of this year," he said. "Right now buying 12-month bonds would be extreme and three-year would be more extreme...(Investors) need relatively stable exchange rate forecasts."
But with the IMF money and a passed budget, investors may feel more comfortable investing longer-term in Ukraine, knowing what targets have been set.
The draft 1997 budget forecasts annual inflation at 24 to 25 percent this year, although Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko said last month it would be no higher than 15 to 16 percent.
The hryvnia on Tuesday was unchanged at 1.8570 to the dollar on the Ukraine Interbank Currency Exchange.
Ukreximbank dealer Valentyn Lebed said inflation risks made the bonds less attractive than discount Treasury-bills, sold weekly in maturities of three-, six-, nine- and 12-months.
"Non-residents would only buy them in the event they would know the hryvnia's rate when the bond matures," he said.
"Nine percent is a good rate in highly-developed countries," he added.
Deputy Prime Minister Serhiy Tyhypko, in charge of reforms, said the trading band for the hryvnia had been implemented but last month, Lazarenko called its existence into question.

Alexander Okhrymenko, a dealer at Banque Societe Generale Ukraine, said long-term bonds were a good idea and would meet demands by foreign investors, but said 15-percent annual interest was unrealistic.
Okhrymenko also said Ukrainians lacked the cash for long-term bonds, to be sold at a nominal value of 100 hryvnias each.

Yields on sales of T-bills last week stood at 20.13 percent for six-month paper, 28.13 percent for nine-month paper and 30.46 for one-year paper. The Finance Ministry tried selling 18-month Treasury bills in April but none was bought.
